NtAllocateVirtualMemory.description: Allocates a region of virtual memory in the address space of a process
NtAllocateVirtualMemory.why_edr_hooks: First step in every shellcode injection. EDR hooks this to detect memory allocation with RWX permissions or suspicious size ranges
NtAllocateVirtualMemory.hook_location: ntdll.dll export table - first 5 bytes patched with JMP to EDR handler
what_edr_checks: Memory protection flags - RWX allocation is immediately suspicious
Allocation size - very large or very specific sizes match known shellcode loaders
Calling process - allocation from an unusual parent process raises alerts
Frequency - rapid repeated allocations indicate shellcode staging

evasion_confidence.explanation: Confidence drops against kernel-level EDRs that monitor syscall patterns rather than just user-mode hooks

NtWriteVirtualMemory.description: Writes data into the virtual address space of a target process
NtWriteVirtualMemory.why_edr_hooks: Used to write shellcode into previously allocated memory. EDR correlates this with NtAllocateVirtualMemory calls to detect injection chains
NtWriteVirtualMemory.hook_location: ntdll.dll export table - first 5 bytes patched with JMP to EDR handler
what_edr_checks: Target process - writing into another process memory is highly suspicious
Data content - entropy analysis to detect shellcode patterns
Correlation - is this following an NtAllocateVirtualMemory call on same region
Write size - matches known payload sizes

evasion_confidence.explanation: Behavioural correlation between Allocate and Write calls is the main detection vector even with syscall bypass

NtProtectVirtualMemory.description: Changes the protection attributes of a region of virtual memory
NtProtectVirtualMemory.why_edr_hooks: Without changing memory to executable the shellcode cannot run. EDR watches for RW to RX transitions which indicate staged shellcode execution
NtProtectVirtualMemory.hook_location: ntdll.dll export table - first 5 bytes patched with JMP to EDR handler
what_edr_checks: Protection change direction - RW to RX or RWX is the classic shellcode pattern
Region origin - was this region previously written to by NtWriteVirtualMemory
Process context - protection changes in remote processes are flagged
Memory address - known shellcode staging address ranges

evasion_confidence.explanation: The RW to RX transition is one of the strongest behavioural indicators. Even with syscall bypass the pattern remains visible to kernel callbacks

NtCreateThreadEx.description: Creates a thread that runs in the virtual address space of another process
NtCreateThreadEx.why_edr_hooks: The execution trigger. EDR hooks this as the final step of process injection to catch shellcode at the moment it is launched
NtCreateThreadEx.hook_location: ntdll.dll export table - first 5 bytes patched with JMP to EDR handler
what_edr_checks: Start address - does the thread start address point to previously written memory
Target process - remote thread creation is always suspicious
Thread flags - specific flags indicate injection attempts
Call chain - correlates with prior Allocate and Write calls on same target

evasion_confidence.explanation: Remote thread creation into another process is one of the most monitored behaviours. Kernel ETW callbacks catch this even when user-mode hooks are bypassed

NtOpenProcess.description: Opens an existing process and returns a handle to it
NtOpenProcess.why_edr_hooks: Required to access another process before injection. EDR hooks this to detect when a process tries to open sensitive targets like lsass or security tools
NtOpenProcess.hook_location: ntdll.dll export table - first 5 bytes patched with JMP to EDR handler
what_edr_checks: Target process - opening lsass, security tools, or privileged processes is flagged
Access rights - PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS or VM_OPERATION rights indicate injection intent
Calling process - unexpected processes opening sensitive targets
Frequency - rapid process handle acquisition indicates enumeration or injection prep

evasion_confidence.explanation: Handle acquisition patterns are visible at kernel level regardless of how the syscall is invoked
